hook: A figure skater, a tightrope walker’s long pole and a baseball bat held by the wrong end all show the same thing. How hard something is to set turning depends on where its mass sits, not just how much there is. Move the same mass farther from the axis and it fights a change in rotation much harder.

chain.cause: Every bit of mass in a turning object moves in a circle about the axis
chain.effect: it resists changes in that motion in proportion to its mass

chain.cause: Mass farther from the axis moves faster for a given ω
chain.effect: it counts more, as the square of its distance

chain.cause: Adding mr² for every bit of mass
chain.effect: gives the rotational inertia I = Σmr², in kg·m²

ideas: Rotational inertia I = Σmr² is the rotational partner of mass: it measures resistance to a change in rotation.
r is each mass’s distance from the axis, and it is squared: doubling r gives 4 times the I.
Same mass, different distribution, different I. A hoop (MR²) beats a disk (½MR²) of the same M and R.
Inertias of disks, rods, hoops and spheres are given on the exam; you do not memorize them.
Parallel-axis theorem: I = I<sub>cm</sub> + Md². I is least about the center of mass.

misconception.wrong: Two objects with the same mass have the same rotational inertia.
misconception.right: Rotational inertia depends on where the mass is. A hoop and a disk of equal mass and radius differ by a factor of 2, and the same rod is 4 times harder to turn about its end than about its middle.

summary: Rotational inertia I measures how hard an object is to set turning about an axis. For point masses I = Σmr², so it depends on both the mass and how far the mass is from the axis, with distance counted squared. The inertias of standard shapes are given. About an axis a distance d from the center of mass, I = I_cm + Md².
